description:
Description:
The accommodation is approached through an entrance hallway and includes a well-proportioned living room and dining room, together with a more modern kitchen/living/dining area and a conservatory overlooking the rear garden. A particularly interesting feature of the property is the separate entrance to the front, which leads through a charming tunnel area to the conservatory, adding both character and versatility to the layout.

Throughout the house, many original architectural features remain, providing a wonderful sense of history and character while allowing scope for modernisation and personalisation. The generous accommodation and three-storey layout make this an ideal family home, city residence, boutique hotel or potential investment opportunity, subject to the necessary planning considerations.

To the rear, the property benefits from a private paved garden, thoughtfully arranged with a combination of seating areas and raised flower beds, creating an attractive and manageable outdoor space with a large block built garden shed. Rear lane access is an additional advantage, providing valuable private parking for two cars â€” a rare and highly desirable feature for a property in such a central city location.

Combining period architecture, generous accommodation, private parking and an enviable position overlooking the Tholsel, this is a remarkable property that offers a rare opportunity to acquire a substantial historic residence in the very heart of Kilkenny.

Outside:
The rear yard is finished with low-maintenance paved flooring and is enhanced by a selection of raised flower beds, providing colour and interest throughout the year.
A roller shutter door offers secure and convenient access directly from the rear laneway, making the space ideal for vehicle access, or a variety of practical uses.
A substantial block-built garden shed (2.38m x 5.10m) provides excellent additional storage or workshop space. Fully powered and set on a solid concrete floor, the building offers a versatile space.

Services:
Mains Gas supply to hob and fireplace with oil fired central heating , mains water and mains sewerage.

** The renowned Kilkenny architect William Robertson (1770â€“1850) was responsible for the design and construction of No. 12 William Street, where he also lived. Built in the early 1800s, the house is a fine example of Robertsonâ€™s architectural work in the city. Its distinctive entrance porch, constructed from locally quarried Kilkenny limestone, is characteristic of his style and reflects his use of the countyâ€™s celebrated stone in both practical and decorative ways.
Robertson studied architecture in Dublin and London before returning to his native Kilkenny, where he established himself as one of the most influential architects of his generation. Over the course of his career, he was involved in the design, construction and remodelling of many important buildings throughout Kilkenny city and county.

Among the buildings associated with Robertson are the Court House, the Gaol, Jenkinstown House, Ormonde College, St Caniceâ€™s Church, the Methodist Church and Tinnypark House. His work extended beyond new construction to the sensitive remodelling of existing historic buildings. At Kilkenny Castle, for example, he introduced oriel windows to the Long Hall, adding a distinctive architectural feature that he later echoed in his own home.

Robertson designed Rosehill House for himself and his wife, incorporating oriel windows similar to those he had used at Kilkenny Castle. Rosehill House, now incorporated into Hotel Kilkenny, provides another important insight into his architectural style and personal taste.
Beyond his architectural achievements, Robertson was an active and respected member of Kilkenny society. He was a supporter of Catholic Emancipation and served as Mayor of Kilkenny in 1831. His contribution to the architectural character of the city and county, together with his civic involvement, ensured that he became a much-respected figure in nineteenth-century Kilkenny.

No. 12 William Street therefore has a particular significance not only as a historic early nineteenth-century house, but also through its direct association with one of Kilkennyâ€™s most notable architects. The building offers a tangible connection to William Robertsonâ€™s professional work, his architectural language and his life in the city he helped to shape.
